title: Humbly and in secret
hook: call on your Lord humbly and privately, with fear and hope (7:55–56)

segments.voice: Yesterday: israf, going past the limit. Your line was enough, no waste. Today, a limit of another kind: how loud to be when you call on God.

On a journey with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, his companions climbed a hill and, the way travelers do, shouted Allahu akbar into the valley at the top of their lungs. A report in Bukhari says he told them, gently, to take it easy on themselves. You're not calling someone deaf, he said, or someone far away. You're calling one who hears, and who is near. Grown men, mid-shout, lowering their voices. Surah seven, verse fifty-five, says the same thing as a command.
screen: `SHOUTING INTO THE VALLEY.` → `NOT DEAF, NOT FAR AWAY.` → `ONE WHO HEARS, AND IS NEAR.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's words: “Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret. Lo! He loveth not aggressors.” Two Arabic words carry the manner. Tadarru'an: humbly, with the pleading of someone who really needs something. Khufyatan: hidden, privately, under your breath. The prophet Zakariyya does exactly this in surah nineteen: an old man calling his Lord in a secret call, asking quietly for a child. The verse then warns that Allah doesn't love those who overstep. Commentators gave examples of overstepping in du'a: shouting, praying for something harmful, or demanding absurd detail. A report in Abu Dawud tells of a companion who heard his son ask for the white palace on the right side of paradise, and told him to ask simply for paradise. The next verse adds two more words: call on Him in fear and hope, khawfan wa tama'an. Not only fear, which can crush; not only hope, which can turn careless. Both, like two wings of a bird, as some scholars put it. And the verse ends: the mercy of Allah is near to those who do good. Near: the same thing the Prophet said on the hill. In this teaching, a quiet du'a needs no audience, no microphone, no perfect Arabic. It can happen at a red light, in the shower, at two in the morning. The verse asks only that it be humble, and that it be yours.
screen: `TADARRU' — HUMBLY, PLEADING.` · `KHUFYAH — HIDDEN, UNDER THE BREATH.` · `DON'T OVERSTEP.` · `FEAR AND HOPE, TWO WINGS.` · then, large: `HUMBLY AND IN SECRET.`

segments.voice: Let your voice go quiet, even inside your head, and name plainly one thing you actually need: health for someone, a way through a problem, a softer heart. If you pray, make a du'a for it now in your own words, under your breath; if you don't, hold that need quietly, with a little fear and a little hope.
Tadarru'an, humbly, the way someone pleads when they truly need something. Call on your Lord that way, and in secret, in fear and hope, for His mercy is near. Today's word.
Your line: humbly, in secret. The One you're calling hears, and is near. Four hundred eight days now.

howItsDone: Muslims make du'a, personal supplication, at any time and in any language, often quietly after the prayer or in prostration; teachers cite 7:55 for keeping it humble and low-voiced.

chat.says: Do I have to pray out loud, in perfect Arabic, for God to hear me?
options: No: 7:55 says call on your Lord humbly and in secret. He hears, and He is near.
Yes, a du'a only counts if it's said loudly enough for other people to hear it.
No, but He only hears a du'a that's made inside a mosque.
chat.meaning: Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret (7:55). The Prophet told shouting companions they were calling one who hears and is near.

Tadarru'an.meaning: humbly, pleading like someone in real need

Zakariyya.meaning: the prophet who asked quietly for a child

du'a.meaning: a personal prayer, calling on God

notes: Hadith numbers (Bukhari 2992; Abu Dawud 96) cited from memory; confirm. The Bukhari report's setting (climbing a hill / valley) is paraphrased; confirm details.
'Two wings of a bird' for fear and hope is a saying attributed to various scholars, given as 'some scholars put it'; confirm.
Practice invites a du'a in the listener's own words 'if you pray'; no prayer text is written.
